one_liner: Header-only C++ compact Hist-Tree: a flattened radix-histogram table over sorted integer keys, beating RMI/PGM/RadixSpline lookup latency.
what_it_does: A static index over a sorted array of unique uint32_t/uint64_t keys. You give a Builder the min key, the max key, a bin count (a power of two) and a max error, call AddKey on every key in ascending order, and Finalize into an immutable CompactHistTree. GetSearchBound(key) returns a [begin, end) window of at most max_error+1 positions, and you run your own std::lower_bound or linear scan inside it. The interface has the same Builder/AddKey/Finalize/GetSearchBound shape as RadixSpline's, but it is not a container: it stores no keys or values and cannot be updated.
how_it_is_fast: Each node is an equal-width histogram over a power-of-two key range, so picking a bin is one right shift of (key - min) instead of a comparison or a model evaluation. Bins holding more than max_error keys get a child node, and the rest are terminal. The compact layout flattens all nodes into one array of 32-bit cells. A terminal bin stores the prefix-sum position, flagged in bit 31, and an inner bin stores its child's row, so each level of a lookup is a shift, a load and a flag test. The configurations that tune best use high bin counts, which keeps the tree to a few levels. An optional cache-oblivious (van Emde Boas-style recursive) node order is provided for deep trees, meaning small bin counts or small errors.
when_to_use: Read-only, sorted, duplicate-free 32- or 64-bit unsigned integer keys (SOSD-style books, fb or osm distributions) where lowest lookup latency matters and you can rebuild when the data changes.
You can afford a large index. In an independent evaluation it was the fastest index on books, fb and osmc at 200M keys, but only from about 100 MiB of index upward.

Skewed or clustered key distributions where RadixSpline's single radix table degenerates. The PLEX authors' auto-tuner picked CHT over a radix table on the face dataset for exactly this outlier problem.
You want a tiny, dependency-free header drop with two knobs. SOSD's tuned fastest configurations are a starting point: 1024 bins with error 16 on books and osm, and 256 bins with error 32 on fb.
You need a secondary radix layer over a small sorted key set, such as spline knots, which is how PLEX uses it.
when_not_to_use: Keys with duplicates. Open issue #4 reports wrong search ranges on SOSD's wiki dataset, and the returned bound can silently miss the key. Both the PLEX and Maltry/Dittrich papers had to exclude wiki.
Any inserts or deletes. The compact layout is build-once. The paper's updatable Hist-Tree is 2-3x slower and is not in this repo.

Tight memory budgets. At smaller index sizes, RMI, PGM-index and RadixSpline beat it in Maltry & Dittrich's evaluation. The table costs nodes x num_bins x 4 bytes, and a small max_error multiplies the node count.
Strings, floats or signed keys. Only uint32_t and uint64_t are tested, and binning relies on unsigned subtraction and shifts.
MSVC/Windows, or when you need a maintained dependency. It uses __builtin_clz/__builtin_clzl, has no releases, has 9 stars and has had no commits since July 2021.

integration.dependencies: none (STL only; CMake fetches GoogleTest 1.10.0 only to build the tests)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (structured bindings, std::optional); GCC or Clang builtins required. Known to build with gcc 9.3 (paper) and clang 12.0.1 (Maltry & Dittrich).
integration.platforms: LP64 targets with GCC/Clang (Linux; macOS/AppleClang since the May 2021 ambiguity fix). The headers have no ISA-specific code, though the repo's CMake adds -march=native. MSVC is not supported.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. GetSearchBound is a const read of an immutable table, so concurrent lookups after Finalize only read. The Builder is single-threaded.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — It has the same Builder(min, max, ...)/AddKey/Finalize/GetSearchBound -> SearchBound{begin, end} shape as RadixSpline, so it swaps into RS- or SOSD-style code. It needs its own num_bins/max_error tuning and unique keys, has no serialization, and offers no RMI- or PGM-compatible API.

gotchas: Input validation is assert-only. Release builds do not catch unsorted keys, min/max that don't equal the first/last key, a num_bins that is not a power of two, or a key range smaller than num_bins, and any of these yields wrong bounds.

Positions and node ids are 31-bit, because bit 31 of each unsigned cell is the leaf flag. That caps the index at about 2.1 billion keys or nodes. A fork (jakubpawlewicz/CHT) adds Builder::CheckFeasible() because some parameter/data combinations make the tree too large.
builder.h uses std::cerr and std::function but includes neither <iostream> nor <functional>. Include both before it or it may fail to compile.

The default two-pass Builder copies every key into its own vector and also keeps per-node bin vectors, so peak build memory is well above the final index size. single_pass=true avoids the key copy, but it is ignored, with only a stderr warning, when use_cache (the cache-oblivious layout) is set.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over RadixSpline, RMI and PGM-index when the data is static and duplicate-free and you can spend a 100 MiB-class index for the lowest probe latency, with builds far cheaper than RMI's optimizer. Pick PLEX instead when you want one hyperparameter, a small index or duplicate keys: it embeds this CHT under a spline and auto-tunes it. For updates, use PGM-index, ALEX or LIPP.
verified_claims_summary: The 1.1-1.8x (RMI), 1.7-2.5x (PGM-index) and 1.2-2.7x (RadixSpline) lookup-latency wins come from Crotty's CIDR 2021 paper. They compare each index's fastest configuration on SOSD's 200M-key amzn/face/osm/wiki sets, compiled with gcc/g++ 9.3.0 (flags unstated) on an AWS c5.4xlarge (Xeon Platinum 8124M), using Crotty's own C implementation rather than this repo. Separately, Maltry & Dittrich (PVLDB 15(5), 2022) benchmarked this exact repo with clang 12.0.1 -O2 on a single thread of a Xeon E5-2620 v4 and found it the fastest index on books, fb and osmc once its index reaches about 100 MiB (graph-only; wiki excluded because of duplicates).
status_note: Abandoned since July 2021 with the duplicate-key bug (#4) still open, but it is MIT-licensed, under 18 KB of headers and still pinned as a SOSD competitor submodule, so vendoring and patching it is realistic.
